description: We’re EmberNova, a team from Giza, Egypt, brought together by a question: how can decades of NASA experiments help crews prepare for fires in space? For the Flame in Freefall challenge, we combined AI, web development, and data visualization to build a research workspace that lets users trace findings back to the original experiments. We also built the Learning Laboratory for students and Space Fire Academy for children to explore the same science through experiments and play.
summary: EmberNova is a web workspace that helps researchers, aerospace engineers and astronauts use NASA combustion experiments to answer spacecraft fire-safety questions. Ask a question in plain language and the research agent finds relevant studies, while backend tools compare conditions and chart values from the original tables. The workspace searches 34 investigations and indexes 1,161 curated rows across 13 tables, including measurements and experimental design data. Users can open citations to inspect the original source, see which conditions differ, and identify where evidence is missing. For example, the Applicability Envelope shows which tests cover a proposed habitat’s oxygen and pressure conditions. Matching those conditions still leaves lunar and Martian gravity untested in the PSI dataset. Built for Flame in Freefall, EmberNova makes scattered NASA data easier to use and helps teams identify which fire-safety questions need new experiments. We also built a Learning Laboratory for students and Space Fire Academy for children, giving the next generation a hands-on way to explore how fire behaves in space.
details:
In 1912, the Titanic struck an iceberg. Some passengers hesitated to leave even as the ship took on water.

But we’re not here to tell the story of the Titanic. We’re here to talk about other ships. Ships that carry people thousands of kilometers from Earth, and could one day take crews millions of kilometers from home. If a fire breaks out that far from Earth, the crew has to act with what they have on board.

In 1997, a fire aboard the Mir space station filled modules with smoke and blocked access to one of the crew’s two escape spacecraft. In space, the difference between having time to act and running out of it can come down to what we learned before launch.

That’s why we built EmberNova. It helps researchers find and rank NASA experiments, see what they reveal about how fire and smoke behave in microgravity, and trace each result back to the original evidence.

Research workspace — a live question and cited answer

Investigation ranking — why a NASA study matched

What EmberNova does

EmberNova gives spacecraft and habitat safety teams one place to explore NASA combustion experiments. Start with a question such as “Which NASA tests are relevant to a lunar habitat at 34% oxygen and about 10 psi?” The workspace shows the closest studies, the experimental conditions they cover, the measurements available, and the evidence gaps.

How it works

The research agent combines keyword and semantic search across 34 investigations, including 25 from NASA’s Physical Sciences Informatics repository and nine supplemental investigations. Backend tools query 1,161 curated rows across 13 tables. The workspace labels the FLEX-2 design matrix as experimental planning data, preserves original values alongside normalized units, and generates measurement charts from source rows. Results explain why studies matched and distinguish direct, indirect and insufficient evidence.

Evidence and scientific limits

Each verified citation opens an evidence record with the source file, its SHA-256 fingerprint, a page or row reference, and any transformation applied. Run comparisons flag differences in test conditions, and the Applicability Envelope shows where measured oxygen and pressure overlap a target atmosphere. Gravity is evaluated separately. The PSI corpus contains no lunar or Martian partial-gravity runs, so extrapolating to those conditions would require new evidence. The Evidence Map helps researchers see where that evidence is missing.

What users can explore

The live site includes recorded walkthroughs, a study browser, a dataset explorer with CSV export, run comparisons, original NASA media, and a fire-safety systems view. Recorded walkthroughs are available without a live model call. Judges can start with Recorded Demos (https://embernova.khedmetak.com/featured), choose “An atmosphere is not a gravity regime,” and open a citation to inspect the exact NASA source.

Learning and play for the next generation

We originally built EmberNova for researchers, aerospace engineers and astronauts. We added two ways for younger learners to build an understanding of the same science and see how they could contribute to safer space missions.

In the Learning Laboratory (https://embernova.khedmetak.com/learn), students work through five guided modules, make predictions, and vary gravity, airflow or oxygen in a virtual combustion chamber. The lessons link to NASA sources and the research workspace.

In Space Fire Academy (https://embernova.khedmetak.com/kids), children explore five rooms on a space station as an astronaut with Pip, a robot guide. They use pretend experiments and tasks like redirecting airflow and inspecting a detector to learn how spacecraft fire safety works. Both experiences label SI-generated content and use conceptual illustrations for the experiments.

Tools and SI disclosure

We built the workspace with Python, FastAPI, SQLite, DuckDB, Parquet, and pint on the backend, and TypeScript, React, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Plotly, and three.js on the frontend. The OpenAI Responses API and embeddings support the research workflow. The optional Analysis Lab runs SI-generated Python in an OpenAI-hosted container and labels its exploratory outputs. We used Claude Code and Codex to assist with architecture, review, implementation, and documentation. In the workspace, SI interpretation is labeled and NASA measurements retain their source provenance. Supporting libraries and tools include Uvicorn, Pydantic, React Router, Radix UI Dialog, react-markdown, remark-gfm, uv, pytest, Ruff, Vitest, ESLint, and Playwright. The live app runs on an Ubuntu VPS with systemd, nginx, and Let’s Encrypt.
